Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: HGMetaADR: a multimodal heterogeneous graph meta-learning framework for generalized adverse drug reaction prediction
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractEarly identification of adverse drug reactions (ADRs), which refer to harmful or unintended responses to medications taken at normal doses, is crucial for reducing clinical trial failures and associated economic costs. However, existing ADR datasets often exhibit a long-tailed label distribution and lack sufficient training examples for rare side effects, making it difficult for vanilla supervised learning models to generalize to underrepresented classes. To address these issues, we propose HGMetaADR, a novel heterogeneous graph-based meta-learning framework for ADR prediction. Built upon a multimodal biomedical knowledge graph, this approach integrates complementary drug-related data, including molecular structures, protein sequences, side effects, and therapeutic indications. It employs a hierarchical attention mechanism to capture semantic dependencies across heterogeneous entities and adopts a model-agnostic meta-learning strategy to enhance adaptation to small-sample classes. We evaluate HGMetaADR under three scenarios—few-shot, zero-shot, and majority—to simulate real-world conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HGMetaADR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, ablation studies and pathway enrichment analyses reveal the underlying biological mechanisms linking protein targets, therapeutic indications, and side effects, thereby validating the effectiveness of incorporating heterogeneous biomedical knowledge into ADR modeling.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search for antimicrobial peptide sequence optimization and in vitro antibacterial assessment
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractThe rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens necessitates the development of novel therapeutic agents, yet the de novo design of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) is challenged by the vast combinatorial search space and the difficulty of balancing efficacy with toxicity. To address these limitations, we introduce a reinforcement learning framework that employs surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search to explore the peptide landscape. By integrating surrogate models for predicted antimicrobial activity, HemoDL-predicted hemolytic propensity, and ESMFold structural confidence, the system performs multi-property computational optimization and candidate prioritization. In silico analysis demonstrated that the optimized peptides adopt amphipathic α-helical structures with high predicted folding confidence and possess favorable docking scores against Staphylococcus aureus resistance targets, including PBP2a and MurA. To assess the biological relevance of the computationally prioritized candidates, 16 peptides were synthesized and evaluated by agar dilution against a 37-strain bacterial panel over a concentration range of 0.25–64 μg/ml. AMP2, AMP7, and AMP9 achieved complete inhibition of at least one tested strain, corresponding to 3 of 16 synthesized candidates (18.75%). AMP12 and AMP13 showed partial growth reduction without complete inhibition within the tested range, whereas the remaining 11 candidates showed no complete inhibition. These findings quantify the current gap between surrogate-defined computational enrichment and assay-specific antibacterial activity. The strain-dependent experimental outcomes further indicate that surrogate, docking, and structural scores do not fully capture all determinants of antibacterial efficacy. The experimental assessment was limited to bacterial agar-dilution activity; mammalian-cell cytotoxicity, wet-lab hemolysis, and peptide-stability assays were not performed. In conclusion, this study establishes a computational framework for the design of bioactive peptides and provides structural insights for bridging the gap between deep learning predictions and experimental outcomes.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: GLAlign integrates single-cell multi-omics data via global manifold and local marker gene alignment
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractIntegrating heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics datasets remains challenging because different modalities are measured in distinct feature spaces and lack cell level pairing. Existing manifold alignment or feature conversion framework are often affected by weak cross-modality associations, geometric ambiguity, and overcorrection. Here we present GLAlign (Global manifold and Local marker gene Alignment), an optimization framework that jointly leverages global manifold structure and local marker gene information to integrate single-cell multi-omics data. GLAlign learns a shared latent space through a global objective comprising maximum mean discrepancy, distortion, and penalty terms, together with a local contrastive triplet loss guided by cross-modality marker gene overlap between independently inferred clusters. We demonstrate GLAlign’s methodological contribution in extending the manifold alignment by biologically informed prior to ensure geometrically plausible and biologically correct alignments without requiring paired cells or manual cell type annotations. We evaluated GLAlign on simulated data and real datasets spanning PBMC scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq, mouse brain SNARE-seq, single-donor and multi-batch CITE-seq, and NCI-N87 scDNA-seq/scRNA-seq integration. Across the evaluated datasets, GLAlign achieved strong modality mixing and biological conservation, remained stable under moderate cell type imbalance and variations in clustering and marker information, and supported cross-modality label transfer and paired cell recovery. These results demonstrate that biologically structured coupling of global and local alignment provides an interpretable framework for heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics integration. GLAlign is freely available at https://github.com/Bateer-Bio/GLAlign.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Biosemantic graph transfer learning for cross-patient cell type annotation and cell–cell interaction analysis in tumor single-cell RNA sequencing
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractThe exploration of cellular heterogeneity within the tumor microenvironment (TME) via single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is essential for understanding cancer progression and response to therapy. Current scRNA-seq approaches, however, lack spatial context and rely on incomplete datasets of ligand–receptor interactions, limiting accurate cell type annotation and cell–cell communication inference. This study addresses these challenges using a novel graph neural network model that enhances cell-type prediction and cell-interaction analysis. Our study utilized a dataset consisting of 49 024 cells from 19 patients across three cancer types: leukemia, breast invasive carcinoma, and colorectal cancer. The proposed scGSL model demonstrated robust performance, achieving an average accuracy of 84.83%, precision of 86.23%, recall of 81.51%, and an F1 score of 80.92% across all datasets. These metrics represent a significant enhancement over existing methods, which typically exhibit lower performance metrics. Additionally, by reviewing existing literature on gene interactions within the TME, the scGSL model proves to robustly identify biologically meaningful gene interactions in an unsupervised manner, validated by significant expression differences in key gene pairs across various cancers. The source code and data used in this study can be found at https://github.com/LiYuechao1998/scGSL.

Genome Biology.title: G-quadruplex profiling using single-cell CUT&Tag offers insight into the epigenetic landscape of the developing mouse brain
Genome Biology.abstract: Background G-quadruplexes (G4s) are non-canonical DNA structures that have gained increasing attention for their potential roles in gene regulation and role in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Despite their biological significance, G4 structures have not been studied systematically across tissues and cell types. Results In this study, we employ G4 single-cell CUT&Tag (G4 scCUT&Tag) to characterize G4 landscapes in postnatal mouse brain cells, leveraging single-cell analytical approaches commonly used in scRNA-Seq and scATAC-Seq datasets. Using conventional single-cell omics workflows to process and explore our data, we distinguish distinct cell lineages based on G4 heterogeneity and establish that a subset of lineage-specific genes show unique promoter G4s. Multi-omics integration with scRNA-Seq gene expression profiles, using both a covariance-based technique (canonical correlation analysis) and a transfer learning-based approach, enables more accurate cell-type annotation. These integrations not only reveal correlations between G4 signal and gene expression, but demonstrate that G4 scCUT&Tag enables detailed examination of G4 heterogeneity in complex tissues and supports integrative analysis of G4 profiles with other omics layers, offering new insights into the epigenomic landscapes of the developing brain. Conclusions Our findings establish G4 scCUT&Tag as a framework for investigating the cellular heterogeneity of G4 landscapes in complex tissues and provide a basis for exploring their relationships with gene regulation and other layers of chromatin organization.

Genome Biology.title: Structure-guided engineering of eukaryotic Fanzor-ωRNA system enhances in vivo gene editing for dystrophin restoration in a Duchenne mouse model
Genome Biology.abstract: Background Eukaryotic Fanzor (Fz) proteins are compact RNA-guided endonucleases homologous to prokaryotic TnpB/Cas12, offering theoretical advantages for single AAV delivery. However, their low editing efficiency and poorly defined specificity in mammals have hindered therapeutic development. Results Here, we perform structure-guided engineering of Spizellomyces punctatus Fanzor1 nuclease (SpuFz1) to enhance its utility for in vivo genome editing and identify several Fanzor variants whose efficiencies are comparable or only slightly lower than widely-used miniature enAsCas12f1 and large-sized SpCas9. We demonstrate that catalytically dead dSpuFz1-v4.2 can be repurposed for CRISPRa-mediated transcriptional activation in a proof-of-concept manner. Genome-wide PEM-seq in mice reveal low translocation frequencies (below 0.05%, much lower than the background threshold set by the PEM-seq protocol), with no detected events attributable to off-target editing. GUIDE-seq analysis also confirms genome-wide low off-target profile for SpuFz1-v4.2 in human cells, with small amounts of off-target editing due to 3’ terminal sequence tolerability. Embryonic mRNA injection efficiently generates mutant mice. Crucially, single AAV9 delivery of SpuFz1-v4.2 in a humanized Duchenne muscular dystrophy model induces targeted exon skipping, restores dystrophin expression to ~ 10% of wild-type levels, and improves muscle contractile force. Conclusions Structure-guided optimization overcomes the activity barrier of eukaryotic Fanzors while maintaining low off-target effect. The engineered SpuFz1-v4.2 retains the hypercompact size necessary for single AAV packaging, establishing a robust platform for in vivo gene editing. This work positions Fanzor by a preliminary proof-of-concept therapeutic study as a viable, miniature alternative to CRISPR-Cas systems for genetic disease intervention and functional genomics.

Biogeosciences.title: Spatial modelling of available aluminum in glacial till: informing a boreal forest soil carbon predictor
Biogeosciences.abstract: Spatial modelling of available aluminum in glacial till: informing a boreal forest soil carbon predictor Scout M. Quinn, Benjamin Misiuk, Mackenzie E. Patrick, and Susan E. Ziegler Biogeosciences, 23, 8275–8288, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8275-2026, 2026 Boreal forest soils store approximately one third of forest soil carbon globally. Stabilization of organic carbon in these soils is largely controlled by reactive aluminum content derived from parent material, which in boreal regions is typically glacial till. We used a Random Forest approach to predictively map and model reactive aluminum and its uncertainty in glacial till across Newfoundland. This supports future modelling efforts and estimates of the soil carbon reservoir in boreal forests.

Biogeosciences.title: Morphological and phylogenic variability of red snow algae in snowpacks along a glacial valley in Alaska
Biogeosciences.abstract: Morphological and phylogenic variability of red snow algae in snowpacks along a glacial valley in Alaska Masato Ono, Kino Kobayashi, Takumi Suzuki, Ryohei Abe, Suzunosuke Usuba, Jun Uetake, and Nozomu Takeuchi Biogeosciences, 23, 8259–8273, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8259-2026, 2026 We studied red snow in Alaska to learn why these blooms vary in their microscopic life. By examining snow using microscopes and genetic analysis, we found that the ground beneath, either glacier ice or soil, dictates which algae grow. Algae on ice were mostly round, while those on soil were larger and had diverse shapes. Factors like snow depth mattered more than nutrients. This proves the underlying surface acts as a reservoir for life, shaping how red snow develops.

Biogeosciences.title: Growing-season variability and environmental controls of CH4 and N2O fluxes across high-latitude terrestrial ecosystems
Biogeosciences.abstract: Growing-season variability and environmental controls of CH4 and N2O fluxes across high-latitude terrestrial ecosystems Johannes Niemi, Miska Luoto, Anna-Maria Virkkala, Johanna Lehtinen, and Jenni Hultman Biogeosciences, 23, 8289–8317, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8289-2026, 2026 We present 1273 greenhouse gas flux measurements from 144 locations across subarctic wetlands, tundra, and forests. Fluxes were strongly linked with soil temperature, moisture, and pH with pronounced seasonal variation. Key findings include significant N₂O sinks and CH₄ emissions from wetlands, increasing CH₄ emissions from degrading permafrost, and small but consistent CH₄ sinks in forest and tundra. These results help in reducing uncertainties in global greenhouse gas budgets and measurements.
